title: How to Choose an Air Purifier for Allergies
h1: How to Choose an Air Purifier for Allergies
description: Choose an air purifier for allergies by matching room size, HEPA filtration and CADR, and avoiding ozone. Compare portable and whole-home purifier options.
quick_answer: Pick an air purifier with a true HEPA filter, a clean air delivery rate (CADR) suited to the room's size, and no ozone output. Portable units work well for bedrooms. Whole-home purifiers installed in your HVAC system clean the air in every room the ducts reach. Match the purifier to your main triggers, such as pollen, pet dander, dust or smoke.
body:
What allergens are you trying to remove?

Start with what bothers you most. Different purifiers handle different problems:

  • Pollen is fairly large and easy to catch with a good mechanical filter.
  • Pet dander is smaller and lingers in the air, so strong filtration and steady airflow matter.
  • Dust and dust mite debris settle quickly, so frequent vacuuming helps as much as the purifier.
  • Wildfire smoke includes very fine particles plus odors. A HEPA filter catches the particles, and an activated carbon filter helps with smell.
  • Mold spores can be captured by HEPA filters, but the moisture source still needs fixing.

What features matter most?

True HEPA filtration. HEPA filters capture a very high share of fine particles. Look for "true HEPA" rather than vague terms like "HEPA-type" or "HEPA-style," which aren't held to the same standard.

CADR. Clean air delivery rate tells you how much filtered air the unit puts out. Higher CADR means it cleans a room faster. Manufacturers usually list the room size each model is meant for.

Room size. Buy a purifier rated for a room at least as large as yours. A small unit in a big living room won't keep up.

Carbon filter. Useful if smoke, cooking odors or pet smells bother you.

Noise. If it's going in a bedroom, check the noise level on the setting you'll actually use overnight.

What should you avoid?

  • Ozone generators. Ozone can irritate the lungs and make asthma worse. Avoid units that intentionally produce ozone.
  • Vague marketing. Claims about "eliminating" allergens without specific filter types or ratings are a warning sign.
  • Undersized units. A purifier that's too small for the room works hard and does little.
  • Hard-to-find filters. Check that replacement filters are easy to buy before you choose a model.

In California, air cleaning devices sold for indoor use must meet state ozone emission limits, so look for that certification on the box.

Portable purifier or whole-home system?

A portable purifier cleans one room. It's a good fit for a bedroom, a home office or a nursery, and you can move it around. Many people with allergies start with a portable unit in the bedroom, since that's where they spend the most hours.

A whole-home purifier is installed in your HVAC system and treats the air every time the system runs. It works best in homes with central air and well-sealed ducts. It's out of sight, quiet, and covers every room the ducts reach. Options include high-efficiency media filter cabinets and other in-duct air cleaners.

Our indoor air quality service installs whole-home purifiers and can help you decide whether one fits your system or whether a portable unit makes more sense.

How do you get the most from an air purifier?

  1. Place a portable unit where it has open space around it, not tucked behind furniture.
  2. Run it continuously on a lower setting rather than blasting it occasionally.
  3. Keep doors and windows closed while it runs, especially on high-pollen or smoky days.
  4. Replace filters on the schedule the manufacturer recommends.
  5. Keep your HVAC filter fresh too, since the two work together.

Do local conditions change the choice?

A bit. Santa Ana winds and wildfire season make smoke and fine dust a bigger concern, which favors HEPA filtration paired with carbon. Coastal homes with damp air may notice more mold and dust mites, so humidity control helps the purifier do its job.

Spring pollen can be heavy here. If your allergies peak in spring, have your purifier and HVAC filter ready before the season starts.

How do you compare purifiers side by side?

When you've narrowed it down to a few models, line them up on the same few points: the room size each is rated for, CADR, filter type, the cost and availability of replacement filters, noise on low and medium settings, and whether it carries California ozone certification. Leave out features you won't use, like app controls you'll never open.

The best purifier is the one sized correctly, quiet enough to leave running, and easy to keep in fresh filters. A cheaper unit you run every day will do more than an expensive one sitting off in a corner.
faqs: Do air purifiers really help with allergies?

They can reduce airborne allergens like pollen, pet dander and smoke particles, which may ease symptoms for many people. They work best alongside regular cleaning, a good HVAC filter and controlling humidity.
Should I run my air purifier all the time?
Running it continuously on a moderate setting usually works better than turning it on only when symptoms flare. Allergens keep entering the air, so steady filtration keeps levels lower.
Is a whole-home air purifier better than a portable one?
A whole-home system treats every room the ducts reach and is out of sight. A portable unit is cheaper to start with and works well in one room. Many allergy-prone homes use both.
How often do purifier filters need changing?
It depends on the model and how dusty the home is. Follow the manufacturer's schedule and check filters more often during wildfire smoke or pollen season.
